rules: The National Polygon Service contains three licensed chargeable datasets: National Polygon, Title Descriptor, and Title Number and UPRN Look Up.
The National Polygon dataset shows the indicative shape and position of each boundary of a registered title for land and property in England and Wales.
HM Land Registry states that every freehold or leasehold title has at least one index polygon in the National Polygon dataset.
The National Polygon dataset contains more than 25 million titles and 28 million polygons.
HM Land Registry states that National Polygon index polygons are mapped against Ordnance Survey MasterMap large-scale mapping.
The National Polygon dataset includes shape, polygon identification, title number, polygon creation date, update date, polygon-version number and record status.
The Title Descriptor dataset records estate interest and class of title for registered estates and interests in England and Wales.
Each registered estate or interest has a unique title number in the Title Descriptor dataset.
HM Land Registry states that one title number can have only one class of title.
An application awaiting registration can have an associated title number before estate-interest or class-of-title information is available.
The Title Descriptor registered-status field distinguishes pending applications from titles that are already registered.
The Title Number and UPRN Look Up dataset links HM Land Registry title numbers with Ordnance Survey AddressBase UPRNs.
The Title Number and UPRN Look Up dataset covers registered properties where the registered address can be associated with an address containing a UPRN.
HM Land Registry links registration addresses with Ordnance Survey AddressBase addresses where a reliable match can be made.
A title number and UPRN are linked only where HM Land Registry can establish a relationship between the AddressBase address and the registered title.
In the Title Number and UPRN Look Up specification the UPRN is the integer identifier of a spatial address.
HM Land Registry's current data catalogue describes the National Polygon Service as a paid annual service requiring an account.
The same HM Land Registry catalogue describes INSPIRE Index Polygons as a free monthly Open Government Licence GML dataset with no API.
INSPIRE Index Polygons contain locations of registered freehold property and are a subset of HM Land Registry's wider Index Polygons database.
HM Land Registry states that absence of a Land Registry-INSPIRE ID may indicate unregistered land, leasehold registration, or another tenure excluded from INSPIRE.
The Tree Preservation Order specification was updated on 10 April 2026.
The Tree Preservation Order specification requires separate tree-preservation-order, tree-preservation-zone and tree datasets.
The tree-preservation-order dataset is specified as CSV, while zone and individual-tree data may use CSV, GeoJSON, GML or GeoPackage.
Planning Data allows specified planning datasets to be served through an OGC WFS or ArcGIS API as well as file downloads.
Planning Data accepts field names written with hyphens, underscores or spaces and normalises uppercase characters to lowercase.
Tree-preservation-order references are required to be unique within the dataset and permanent across updates.
Tree-preservation-zone geometry is specified as a single polygon or multipolygon with points in WGS84.
When planning geometry is supplied in CSV, the geometry is represented as Well-Known Text.
Tree-preservation-zone type is constrained to area, group or woodland.
For tree-preservation records, entry-date represents the last update and equals start-date when the entity has never been updated.
A tree-preservation end-date is left blank while the order remains in effect.
Each individual protected-tree record must provide a point or geometry and may provide both.
Protected-tree point coordinates are specified in the WGS84 coordinate reference system.
When a protected-tree UPRN is supplied, Planning Data requires the address text as well, and vice versa.
The Conservation Area specification was updated on 10 April 2026.
Conservation-area geometry should be supplied in WGS84 where possible; Planning Data warns that transforming other coordinate systems can introduce a small loss of precision.
A conservation-area document-url is intended to point to the authoritative source document for the designation.
Planning Data guidance says an endpoint URL should remain stable when the data is updated; publishers should change the data at the endpoint rather than change the endpoint URL.
Planning Data guidance says historically correct records should not be deleted when they cease to apply; an end date should be added instead.
Planning Data publishing guidance requires an Open Government Licence statement and recommends open data formats rather than relying only on PDF documents.
Environment Agency guidance states that the LIDAR WMS preview is an image of the data and cannot be queried for elevation values.
The Coverage Metadata Files WMS preview shows raster-data extents but not the underlying elevation values.
Environment Agency LIDAR Composite download ZIP files now contain a spatial metadata index in GeoPackage format.
The GeoPackage spatial metadata index describes both the spatial location and temporal extent of the raster elevation data.
For a 1 metre DSM surface model the Environment Agency expects an average point-cloud density of at least one point per square metre across the survey.
The Environment Agency warns that point density contributing to the DTM under vegetation may be lower than the DSM point density.
LIDAR point density varies across a scan and can increase where multiple flight lines overlap.
The Environment Agency states that a LIDAR point cloud is not a regular grid, distinguishing source point density from raster resolution.
The Environment Agency survey download portal supplies LIDAR data in 5 kilometre by 5 kilometre tiles.
The survey download portal can download several tiles at once for relatively small areas.
The Environment Agency states that its portal does not provide a whole-country or very-large-area bulk LIDAR download.
Environment Agency index catalogues include metadata such as the time of year in which source LIDAR was collected.
Environment Agency coverage guidance says its survey index should be used to determine which products cover each grid square.
The Environment Agency LIDAR capture programme includes previous capture seasons as well as the forward look to the current winter season.
Defra metadata guidance says dataset metadata summaries can describe exclusions and known data-quality issues.
Defra metadata records identify applicable use limitations and licence information so suitability can be assessed before use.
Environment Agency WCS global minimum, maximum, mean and standard-deviation values are display statistics and are not candidate-point elevations.
The WCS GeoTIFF NoData sentinel is a transport encoding for missing pixels and must not be treated as a real terrain elevation.
Environment Agency WCS guidance uses the persistent DTM 1m base URL up to the question mark when creating a client WCS layer.
Environment Agency WCS guidance allows the client template extent to be changed, so an exact candidate request must record the requested extent rather than infer it from a preview.
Ordnance Survey describes OS Terrain 50 as a low-resolution digital terrain model with 50 metre post spacing and 10 metre contour intervals.
OS Terrain 50 is produced from photogrammetry and is intended for broad applications over large areas.
The current OS Terrain 50 product page states that the product is updated annually.
The current product page describes OS Terrain 50 as free to use for everyone.
OS Terrain 50 is delivered as grid data with formats including ASCII DTM grid, GML and other supported vector formats for contours.
The OS Terrain 50 technical specification states that contour data includes mean high water and mean low water boundaries as well as spot heights.
OS Terrain 50 grid and contour products are created from the same underlying source data.
Terrain 50 grid and contour data are supplied as 10 kilometre by 10 kilometre tiles identified from the National Grid reference of each tile's south-west corner.
The Terrain 50 grid is a regular grid of heighted points at 50 metre post spacing.
The Terrain 50 contour product uses standard contour polylines at 10 metre intervals.
The source digital terrain model for OS Terrain products is captured as a triangulated irregular network using mass points, breaklines and automated photogrammetric techniques.
Ordnance Survey states that the source TIN can retain feature edges more accurately than a regular grid.
Terrain 50 grid and contour representations are interpolated from the source TIN model.
Ordnance Survey states that Terrain 50 uses a more generalised representation because it is designed to work with small-scale products.
OS OpenData is available for unrestricted free commercial and personal reuse under the Open Government Licence.
The OS Data Hub provides direct download access to OpenData for offline use.
Ordnance Survey describes OS Terrain 50 OpenData as including contours, spot heights, breaklines, coastline, lakes, ridges and formlines.
The Terrain 50 technical specification defines its grid GML as GML 3.2.1 simple-features profile level 0.
Terrain 50 geographic tile downloads are supplied as compressed folders containing the data together with additional supporting files.
OS Downloads API automation guidance warns that product-list items can change and recommends storing the product ID and version so later releases can be detected.

The official DTM1 OGC collection/queryables/sample feature chain is readable, but a TQ2892-filtered survey feature has not yet been read back.
Exact candidate WCS or GeoTIFF bytes, SHA, NoData interpretation and numeric elevations remain absent.
